![](data:image/png;base64,)Multi-sites polycyclodextrin adsorbents for removal of protein-bound uremic toxins combining with hemodialysis

Jingyu Li[a](#_bookmark0), Lulu Han[a](#_bookmark0),[\*](#_bookmark2), Jian Xie[a](#_bookmark0), Shuxin Liu[b](#_bookmark1), Lingyun Jia[a](#_bookmark0),[\*](#_bookmark2)

a _Liaoning Key Laboratory of Molecular Recognition and Imaging, School of Bioengineering, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian 116023, PR China_

b _Nephrology Department, Dalian Municipal Central Hospital, 826 Xinan Road, Dalian 116033, PR China_

A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_ Polycyclodextrin Absorbent

Protein-bound uremic toxins Hemodialysis

A B S T R A C T

Accumulation of protein-bound uremic toxins (PBUTs) has a high incidence in the blood of hemodialysis-treated patients with chronic kidney disease. Development of adsorbent for the high-eﬃcient, selective, and removal of various PBUTs is still challenging because of their strong interactions to the corresponding binding proteins and the complex blood background. Herein, we reported poly-cyclodextrins adsorbents with multi adsorption-sites for PBUTs removal from plasma. Compared to poly-α-cyclodextrin and poly-γ-cyclodextrin, poly-β-cyclodextrin

(PβCD) showed the best adsorption capability and the maximum p-cresol sulfate (PCS, a model PBUT) binding

capacity of PβCD (263 mg g−1). Combining with hemodialysis, PβCD adsorbents added into the dialysate can

remove 96 % PCS in the plasma via adsorbent once-through mode. Additionally, various PBUTs co-exsiting in the plasma could be effectively removed, exhibiting high-concentrition PBUT adsorption property of PβCD. We expect that the PCD adsorbents combining with hemodialysis therapy may become a promising potential for

clinical PBUT removal.

1. Introduction

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) threats the health of 13.4 % of the global population with rising incidence rates and death rates ([Coresh,](#_bookmark21) [2017](#_bookmark21)). CKD patients metabolize and produce many kinds of uremic toxins, which gradually accumulate in the body and lead to further injury of the organisms ([Namekawa, Tokoro Schreiber, Aoyagi, &](#_bookmark37) [Ebara, 2014](#_bookmark37)). Protein-bound uremic toxins (PBUTs), as small mole-cular-weight hydrophobic toxins, have been widely found in the blood of CKD patients, but are poorly eliminated by the clinically used he-modialysis technique due to their strong binding capability to the human serum albumin (HSA) via multiple interactions such as hydro-phobic, electrostatic and van der Waals forces ([Ghannoum, Bouchard,](#_bookmark25) [Nolin, Ouellet, & Roberts, 2014](#_bookmark25); [Tao, Thijssen, Levin, Kotanko, &](#_bookmark42) [Handelman, 2015](#_bookmark42)). Additionally, more and more studies found that the CKD patients, especially, through a long period of hemodialysis, tend to have a high blood concentration of PBUTs which consequently causes higher mortality of the CKD patients than that of the general population ([Chang, Neelakandan, DeFine, Alexander, & Kyu, 2014](#_bookmark19)). For example, p-cresol sulfate (PCS) as a PBUT is commonly traced in the blood of hemodialysis-treated patients and is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases ([Gryp, Vanholder, Vaneechoutte, & Glorieux,](#_bookmark26) [2017](#_bookmark26)). Fortunately, although the binding between PBUTs and human

serum albumin (HSA) is strong, a small ratio of PBUTs reversibly des-orbs from the HSA-PBUT complexes, allowing this free part of toxins to be competitively adsorbed by adsorbents ([Tijink et al., 2012](#_bookmark44)).

An ideal adsorbent should meet the following criteria: (i) high-ef-ficient adsorption of trace amounts of PBUTs in blood, (ii) adsorption of various PBUTs; (iii) selective adsorption to PBUTs other than the background blood proteins, and (iv) safety in clinical applications ([Bhatt & P, 2019](#_bookmark18); [Shao et al., 2018](#_bookmark38); [Tijink et al., 2013](#_bookmark45); [Wei, Han, Ren, &](#_bookmark52) [Jia, 2013](#_bookmark52); [Yang, Han, & Jia, 2016](#_bookmark57)). Over the past decade, two types of absorbents for the removal of PBUTs have been developed. One is mainly based on the hydrophobic interactions between PBUTs and hydrophobic adsorbents such as activated carbon ([Müller, 2010](#_bookmark36)), and the other is based on the size selectivity of porous materials for smaller PBUTs other than larger proteins, such as hemodialysis (HD) hollow fiber membranes ([Yu et al., 2017](#_bookmark58)), zeolite materials and metal-organic framework (MOF) materials ([Kato et al., 2019](#_bookmark29); [Tijink et al., 2013](#_bookmark45)). These adsorbents have achieved some progress but still, exhibit certain setbacks. For example, activated carbon may cause non-specific protein adsorption on its surface that occupies PBUT binding sites, resulting in low PBUT removal and significant loss of beneficial plasma proteins _in vivo_ ([Miller, Hammerschmidt, Anderson, & Moore, 1984](#_bookmark35)). Zeolite ma-terials and some MOFs have a tendency to dissolve in a physiological environment ([De Toni, Jonchiere, Pullumbi, Coudert, & Fuchs, 2012](#_bookmark23);

[Suresh & Matzger, 2019](#_bookmark40)), and additionally, MOFs has limited potential in clinical applications due to the high cost. HD hollow fiber mem-branes are commonly used in the clinical applications for CKD, but achieved only a low PBUTs clearance rate (20 %–50 %) ([Bergé-Lefranc](#_bookmark17) [et al., 2010](#_bookmark17); [Sirich, Funk, Plummer, Hostetter, & Meyer, 2014](#_bookmark39)), due to the above mentioned extremely low concentration of the free PBUTs in the plasma. Thus, developing a safe, low-cost, highly eﬃcient, and competitive adsorption adsorbent for PBUTs removal is still challen-ging.

Recently, our group proposed a new type of water-dispersal ad-sorbent, poly-β-cyclodextrin (PβCD), to be used in combination with hemodialysis system HD hollow fiber membranes as a corresponding removal strategy ([Li et al., 2018](#_bookmark33); [Wang et al., 2012](#_bookmark48)). The major ad-vantage of this strategy is that HD hollow fiber membranes inhibit

plasma protein interaction with adsorbent while allowing PBUT to diffuse from the plasma into the dialysate. To remove the diffusing hydrophobic PBUTs, PβCDs were added in the dialysate of the hemo-dialysis system as an adsorbent and removed 41 % of IS, by host-guest interaction ([Li et al., 2018](#_bookmark33)). Although this manner holds potential in

clinical translation and overcomes certain existing drawbacks such as non-specific protein adsorption and high cost, the removal ratio of PBUTs needs improvement and the adsorption of various PBUTs is untested.

Herein, to enhance the PBUTs removal ratio, we first optimized the inner cavity size of PCDs by synthesizing a series of poly-cyclodextrins (PCDs) through crosslinking reactions between epichlorohydrin (ECH)

and different cyclodextrins, such as α-cyclodextrin (αCD), β-cyclodex-trin (βCD) and γ-cyclodextrin (γCD). To investigate the adsorption capabilities of the PCDs, PCS was first chosen as a model PBUT due to

the highest binding capability to HSA in the blood of all reported PBUTs ([Gryp et al., 2017](#_bookmark26)). Additionally, PCS adsorption kinetics and isotherm, ITC, mechanism of PCDs and competitive binding capability of multi-pocket PCDs against BSA were studied. Furthermore, to optimize the usage of PCDs, PCDs added into the dialysate were used to remove the serum albumin-bound PCS via a recycling mode and once-through mode. Finally, the adsorption of several PBUTs simultaneously present in the plasma by the synthesized PCDs during hemodialysis was in-vestigated. Taken together, we propose this novel PCD adsorbent combining HD blood purification strategy as a promising approach for PBUT removal in the clinic.

1. Materials and method
    1. _Materials_

α-cyclodextrin (αCD), β-cyclodextrin (βCD) and γ-cyclodextrin (γCD) were purchased from Liquan Chemical Industrial Company (Shanxi, China). Para-cresol sulfate (PCS) was purchased from ZZBIO Company (Shanghai, China). Urea and NaCl were bought from Solarbio

(Beijing, China). Epichlorohydrin (ECH) and methylbenzene were ob-tained from Damao Chemical (Tianjin, China). Hippuric acid (HA), quinolinic acid (QA) and acetonitrile (HPLC grade) were bought from J &K Chemical (Beijing, China). Other used chemicals were of analytical grade. Water was purified by a Milli-Q water system (Millipore, Billerica, USA).

- 1.  _Synthesis of PCDs_

CDs were crosslinked because the monomeric CDs could travel through the dialysis membrane and further leak into the plasma during the dialysis therapy, leading to a negative impact on the PBUT removal ([Li et al., 2018](#_bookmark33)). PCDs were synthesized according to a previously re-

ported method ([Li et al., 2018](#_bookmark33)). Briefly, 5.0 g of CD (αCD, βCD or γCD)

and 2.6 g of NaOH were dissolved and mixed in 8 mL of water. Then,

3.5 mL of ECH was added into the mixture. After the crosslinking re-action stirred at 30 °C for 2 h, 30 mL of acetone was added to stop the

reaction. The precipitate was dissolved in water and subsequently neutralized to pH 7 with a diluted hydrochloric acid solution (0.1 mol L−1). The product, defined as PCD, was purified by a filter washing in a high-flux FX80 dialyzer (Fresenius Helixone, Germany) for removing the low-weight monomer and oligomer. The resulting PCDs were stored

at 4 °C before use.

- 1.  _Characterization of poly-cyclodextrins_

Diameters of PαCD, PβCD, and PγCD were measured by a trans-mission electron microscope (TEM, JEOL, Japan). Briefly, 10 μL of

0.5 mg mL−1 PCDs were dropped on a 200-mesh carbon-coated copper

grid. Then, the samples were negatively stained by phosphotungstic acid (2%, w/w) for 1 min and air-dried before used ([Xie, Shi, Du, Cong,](#_bookmark54) [& Zhao, 2016](#_bookmark54)). 1H NMR spectrums of PCDs in D2O were assessed under a Varian INOVA 400 MHz spectrometer (Varian, US).

Contents of effective CDs in PβCD and PγCD were measured by a phenolphthalein decolor experiment, widely used in the titration of CD

because phenolphthalein diving into the cave of CDs transforms from a

pink ionic state into a colorless lactone state (Scheme S1) ([Li et al.,](#_bookmark33) [2018](#_bookmark33)). Briefly, 0.1 mg mL−1 PβCD or PγCD in NaHCO3 buffer (0.1 mol L−1, pH = 10.5) was incubated with 5 mg L−1 phenolphthalein aqu-eous solution for 15 min. After the mixed phenolphthalein solution

changed from pink to colorless, the absorption value of the mixture was measured under the UV–vis spectrophotometer at 550 nm.

Because the cave size of αCD is too small to hold phenolphthalein, αCD content in PαCD was measured by a methylbenzene solubility improvable experiment ([Xie et al., 2016](#_bookmark54)). Briefly, 0.1 mL of methyl-benzene solution was mixed in 1 mL of PαCD (1 mg mL−1) solution. After 10 min vigorous stirring, the absorption value of the mixed PαCD solution was obtained under a UV–vis spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, US) at 261 nm. The effective αCD content in PαCD was cal-culated by a standard curve plotted by using αCD monomer.

The effective CD ratio is defined as the mass ratio of CD capable of binding guest molecule to total CD unit in the PCDs, and calculated by the following equation:

E= Weffective/Wtotal CD (1)

where, E is the effective CD ratio, Weffective is the mass of effective CD measured by the phenolphthalein decolor experiment or methylben-zene solubility improvable experiment, and Wtotal CD is the total mass of CD in the PCDs.

- 1.  _Adsorption kinetics and equilibrium isotherm experiments_

To analyze the PCS adsorption kinetics and equilibrium isotherm of PCDs, different concentrations of PCS were incubated with PCDs at 25 °C. For the adsorption kinetic experiments, PCDs were incubated with PCS with elongated time at a final concentration of 0.5 w/w%

PCDs and 200 mg L−1 PCS, respectively. For the adsorption isotherm

experiment, different initial concentrations of PCS were incubated with

0.5 w/w% PCDs for 2 h. Finally, unbound PCS in the mixture with a lower molecular weight was separated through ultrafiltration (Amicon® Ultra-15, molecular weight cut-off 10 kDa, Merck Millipore, US) at 13,000_g_ centrifuge for 5 min. Finally, the unbound PCS was collected in the filtrate, and the concentration of PCS was measured by the UV–vis spectrophotometer at 264 nm according to the previous study ([de Loor](#_bookmark22) [et al., 2009](#_bookmark22)). The pseudo-first-order equation (Eq. 2), pseudo-second equation (Eq. 3), and the Langmuir model equation (Eq. 4) were ex-pressed as follows ([Kim, Kimura, & Wada, 2019](#_bookmark30); [Tzvetkov, Kaneva, &](#_bookmark46) [Spassov, 2017](#_bookmark46); [Wang et al., 2019](#_bookmark49)):

ln(qe\-qt) = lnqe\-k1t (2)

t/qt = t/k2qe2+t/qe (3)

ce/qe = 1/(k qm)+ce/qm (4)

where, qe (mg g−1) is the capacity of PCD at equilibrium, and qt (mg g−1) is the amount of toxin adsorbed at time t (min). k1 and k2 are the pseudo-first order and pseudo-second order rate constants, respectively. ce is the equilibrium concentration (mg mL−1), qm is the max capacity (mg g−1), and k is the Langmuir constant.

- 1.  _Isothermal titration calorimetry experiments_

Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) experiments were conducted under an ITC200 calorimeter (MicroCal, GE Healthcare, US) at 25 °C. Before measurement, all the solutions were filtered through a 0.22-μm pore size filter. The experiments were performed as 20 injections of

PCD solution (0.2 mmol L−1) into the PCS solution (0.1 mmol L−1), and

0.2 μL of the PCS solution was used for the first injection and 2 μL for all

following injections. The fitting data _K_, _ΔH_ and _ΔS_ were analyzed under Origin 7.0 software (OriginLabs, US) using a single binding site model ([Tapken et al., 2017](#_bookmark43)).

- 1.  _PCS adsorption capability comparison between PCDs and BSA_

PCS (200 mg L−1)-containing PβCD solution (0.5 w/w%) in a dia-lysis bag (Molecular weight cut-off 10 kDa, Solarbio, Beijing, China) was incubated with an equivalent volume of PCS (200 mg L−1)-con-taining BSA solution (0.5 w/w%) for 12 h at room temperature. Then, the concentration of PCS in the PβCD solution by the UV–vis spectro-photometer at 264 nm, while the concentration of PCS in BSA was de-

tected by HPLC ([de Loor et al., 2009](#_bookmark22)). Briefly, 1.5 mL of methanol was added into 0.5 mL of BSA solution. The mixture was vibrated and centrifuged at 13,000_g_ for 3 min. The supernatant was characterized under an Agilent 1200 Series HPLC system at 25 °C and a flow rate of

1 mL min−1 using a C18 column. The mobile phases were gradually mixed by acetonitrile (A) and a pH 4.0 of sodium acetate (10 mmol L−1) buffer (B) from 17.5 % A: 82.5 % B to 45 % A: 55 % B within 8 min. UV

detector setting was set at 264 nm.

- 1.  _PCS removal in plasma using PCD adsorbents in recycling mode_

PCS removal in plasma was evaluated in an _in-vitro_ self-built he-modialysis system. Polysulfone (PSU) micro-dialysis columns (2 mL, micro-dialysis columns for animal use, Wego Holding Co., LTD, China) were used during the dialysis process. 30 mL of plasma containing PCS

(200 mg L−1) and an equivalent volume of dialysate (Tianjin Hao Yang Biological Manufacturer Co., LTD, China) incorporating with 0.5 w/w%

PCD were separately pumped into the lumen and external of the hollow fiber membrane. The flow of the plasma and dialysate was circulatory in the opposite direction at flow rates of 8 mL min−1 and 16 mL min−1, respectively. Herein, the flow rate and used plasma volume were scaled down according to the clinical hemodialysis parameters ([Li et al.,](#_bookmark33)

[2018](#_bookmark33)). The concentration of PCS in plasma was measured by the above mentioned HPLC method except that the BSA solution was replaced by the plasma.

- 1.  _PBUT removal in plasma in once-through mode_

The experiment process of PBUT removal in plasma in once-through mode was similar to Section [2.5](#_bookmark3), except that the dialysate used in a once-through mode without further cycled use.

Apart from the individual PCS PBUT removal, simultaneous removal of various PBUTs was tested. The concentrations of PCS, quinolinic acid

(QA), and hippuric acid (HA) were 200 mg L−1, 500 mg L−1, and 50 mg L−1, respectively. The concentration detection of HA and QA was similar to that of PCS ([Vanholder et al., 2003](#_bookmark47)). However, the mobile

phases were charged with a mixture of methanol (A) and a pH 7.0 of 10 mmol L−1 potassium phosphate buffer (B) in a volume ratio of 1:1. The flow rate was set at 0.9 mL min−1, the column temperature was controlled at 30 °C. UV detector for QA and HA was performed at

272 nm and 238 nm.

- 1.  _Hemocompatibility tests_

The biocompatibility was evaluated by the hemolysis assay and anticoagulant activity using healthy volunteer’s blood ([Wei et al.,](#_bookmark52) [2013](#_bookmark52)). The experiments using blood were performed under the ap-proval of the Local Ethics Committee of the Dalian University of Technology. The hemolysis assay of PCDs was evaluated by the he-molysis rate. Briefly, 0.3 mL of red blood cell suspension was diluted to 6 mL of PBS. 0.2 mL of the diluted red blood cell suspension was in-cubated with 0.8 mL of monomeric CD or PCD PBS solutions, respec-tively. PBS and water were served as negative and positive controls, respectively. After incubation for 2 h at room temperature, the mixtures were centrifuged at 344 _g_ for 5 min to obtain the supernatant, which was further measured under the UV–vis spectroscopy at 541 nm. The hemolysis rate of RBCs was calculated by the following equation:

H(%) = (As\-An)/(Ap\-An) ×100 % (5)

where, H is the hemolysis rate, As is the absorbance of the sample at 541 nm, An is the absorbance of the negative control at 541 nm, and Ap is the absorbance of the positive control at 541 nm.

Anticoagulant activity of PCDs was evaluated by the plasma re-calcification time assay according to reference ([Wei et al., 2013](#_bookmark52)). The platelet-poor plasma (PPP) was obtained by centrifuging fresh blood at

200 _g_ for 10 min and then 2500 _g_ 15 min collecting the final supernate.

0.2 mL of PPP was incubated with 0.8 mL of 0.5 % (w/w) PαCD, PβCD, or PγCD, and 1 mL of 25 mmol L−1 CaCl2. The duration of time of silky fibrin appears in PPP was recorded as plasma recalcification time

(PRT).

- 1.  _Statistical analysis_

Data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical analysis of data was evaluated with Student’s _t_\-test. Statistical significance of data was given at \*_p_ < 0.05 level.

1. Results and discussion
    1. _Synthesis and characterization of PCDs_

To evaluate the effects of cavity size on the binding performances of PCDs, αCD, βCD or γCD monomers were crosslinked with ECH ([Scheme](#_bookmark4) [1](#_bookmark4)), and the crosslinked CDs (PCDs) were designated as PαCD, PβCD,

and PγCD, respectively. TEM images show that the diameters of dry PCDs were 12.2 nm for PαCD (Figure 1a), 13.2 nm for PβCD ([Fig. 1](#_bookmark5)b), and 13.6 nm for PγCD ([Fig. 1](#_bookmark5)c). Moreover, molecular weights of PCDs

measured by gel permeation chromatography were about 90,100 Da for PαCD, 135,000 Da for PβCD, and 93,800 Da for PγCD (Table S1), showing their size and molecular weights are larger than that of HSA ([Chicea, Chicea, & Chicea, 2013](#_bookmark20)). Because the nanopore size of the dialysis membrane is designed smaller than the size of HSA, PCDs en-

dowing larger molecular sizes ([Fig. 1](#_bookmark5)d) could be safely used in the dialysis without leaking through the dialysis membrane into the plasma.

The CDs in the PCDs act as both molecular skeleton and functional groups. The relationship between reacted CDs contents and the toxin-removal level was quantificationally analyzed. 1H NMR results showed reacted molar ratios of CD to ECH in the three PCDs were closely ranged

from 1:1.6 to 1:1.8 ([Fig. 2](#_bookmark6)a). Additionally, the contents of CD (w/w) in the PαCD, PβCD, and PγCD were 88.5 %, 87.3 %, and 87.9 %, re-spectively ([Fig. 2](#_bookmark6) and Table S1), showing that the obtained PCDs mainly consist of CD. Several methods to synthesize cyclodextrin-containing polymers have been developed, such as reaction of CDs with cross-

linking agents or grafting CD on other polymers ([2019b](#_bookmark50), [Alzate-Sánchez](#_bookmark14)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Scheme 1. Schematic illustration of the synthesis process of PCDs.

[et al., 2019](#_bookmark14); [Diget, Städe, & Nielsen, 2019](#_bookmark24); [Wang et al., 2019](#_bookmark49)). Com-pared to the reported CD polymers, the CD contents of which were lower than 70 w/w%, the contents of CD in PCDs were at a higher level (∼ 88 w/w%), which could increase the binding capability of PCDs. Furthermore, even though only about 12 % of hydroxyl-containing

linker (reacted ECH with CDs) was introduced in PCDs, this can sig-nificantly improve the hydrophily and solubility (solubility: 62 g for PαCD, 89 g for PβCD and 71 g for PγCD) of PCDs (Table S1) compared

to the monomeric CDs (solubility: 15 g for αCD, 2 g for PβCD and 23 g

for γCD), that made PCDs more suitable for further usage as water-soluble adsorbents.

After the CDs in PCDs were crosslinked by ECH, the open cavity of the cyclodextrin can be hindered spatially by the connecting ECH, and therefore some of the CDs might be unable to further bind guest toxin molecules. The contents of effective CD (w/w), capable of binding toxin molecule in PCDs, were further investigated. [Fig. 2](#_bookmark6)b exhibited that the effective CD ratios (the ratio of CD capable of binding guest molecule to

total CD unit in the polymer) were reduced to 57 %, 54 %, and 66 % in the PαCD, PβCD, and PγCD, respectively. After the calculation though the molecular weight and the effective CD ratios in each PCDs, the number of effective CDs in a single PCD was 53 for PαCD, 63 for PβCD, and 45 for PγCD (Table S1).

This indicated that only part of the CDs is effective to permit PCDs for further binding guest toxin molecule. The CDs, on the surface of PCDs, prevented guest molecule from diffusing to the core of PCDs, which made some CDs lose their binding ability.

All the above results showed that the resulting three PCDs with different size of cavity exhibited similar characters such as size, mole-cular weight, CD content, and effective CD contents. This can be ex-plained by the fact that the reacted hydroxyl groups of D-glucopyranose in the CDs have a similar chemical environment.

- 1.  _Adsorption kinetics and adsorption isotherm_

To understand the PCS adsorption capability of PCDs, the adsorp-tion kinetics and isotherm were tested. PCS adsorption kinetics of PCDs were evaluated in the PCS aqueous solution with an initial PCS con-centration of 200 mg L−1, the highest concentration of PCS in the pa-tient blood with CKD reported ([Martinez, Recht, Hostetter, & Meyer,](#_bookmark34)

[2005](#_bookmark34)). PCS adsorption of the three PCDs reached equilibrium within 45 min ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark7)a and Figure S1) with PβCD being the fastest. [Fig. 3](#_bookmark7)a shows that PCS adsorption of PβCD reached 67 % of the total saturated

adsorption capability within 15 min ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark7)a), while at the same point of time, the adsorption of PαCD and PγCD merely got to ∼20 %. After

PCS adsorption isotherms of PCDs show the adsorption capability of PCDs increased with an increasing initial PCS concentration, and reached about 107.8 mg g−1, 123.5 mg g−1, and 101.6 mg g−1 for

PαCD, PβCD, and PγCD ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark7)d), respectively. Based on the Langmuir isotherm, the qm of PβCD (263 mg g−1) was higher than that of PαCD (233 mg g−1) and PγCD (238 mg g−1). Compared with other previously reported PBUT adsorbents such as silicalite, cryogels, and porous mixed matrix, PβCD renders the highest qm ([Table 1](#_bookmark8)). In comparison to NU-1000, a MOF material showing a higher PCS removal capability, PβCD

had a lower qm, but still holds greater potential in clinical use as it is composed of safer carbohydrate without the incorporation with the heavy-ion atom ([Table 1](#_bookmark8)).

- 1.  _Comparison of PCS adsorption capability of PCDs and serum albumin_

To effectively remove the HSA-bound PCS in the plasma, PCDs should have PCS adsorption capability that outcompetes serum al-bumin. Herein, we directly compared the PCS adsorption capability of

PβCD and serum albumins using the dialysis bag with a cut-off mole-

cular weight of 1 × 104 Da to allow PCS to travel through the dialysis membrane. Among the PCDs, PβCD with the best PCS adsorption properties was first chosen for the adsorption properties comparison

with BSA ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)a). After 12 h competitive adsorption, we found PCS concentration in the PβCD reached 304 mg L−1 which accounts for 76 ± 4% of total PCS, whereas in the BSA solution PCS concentration reduced to 96 mg L−1, accounting for 24 ± 4% of total PCS ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)a). This result indicated that compared to an equal amount of BSA, PβCD has a higher binding capability to PCS.

Because _in-vivo_ serum albumin concentration in the plasma is close to 4 w/w%, PCS removal rate of 0.5 w/w% PβCD and BSA of a higher concentration (4 w/w%) was studied. We found compared to the 56 % PCS removal for 4 w/w% BSA, the 0.5 w/w% PβCD removed a sig-nificant higher ratio of PCS (67 %, [Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)b). Previously reported studies

found that over 95 % of PCS in the blood may bind to HSA at Sudlow site 2 with an association constant of 1.0 × 105 L mol−1, a value much larger than that of the βCD to PCS ([Watanabe et al., 2012](#_bookmark51)). However, PβCD has 63 functional βCD cavities for PCS adsorption, which endows the presence of multi-pocket binding sites in a single PCD (0.45 mmol g−1) that outcompetes the single binding site in HSA (Sudlow site 2, 0.015 mmol g−1) ([Itoh, Ezawa, Kikuchi, Tsuruta, & Niwa, 2012](#_bookmark27); [Tan](#_bookmark41) [et al., 2017](#_bookmark41); [Yamasaki, Chuang, Maruyama, & Otagiri, 2013](#_bookmark56)). Thus, even used at a lower concentration, PβCD (0.5 %) showed stronger adsorption capability towards PCS than BSA (4%).

- 1.  _Interactions between PCS and PCDs complex_

Next, Job’s plots method was used to probe the adsorption stoi-chiometry of monomeric CDs to PCS. [Fig. 5](#_bookmark10)a shows that all three CDs bind PCS in a 1:1 molar ratio because of size matching between PCS and cavities of CDs. To quantificationally study the binding capability, in-

teractions between PCDs and PCS were further measured under ITC. The association constant (_K_) of PβCD binding PCS was 3.39 × 105 L mol−1, higher than that of PαCD (1.89 × 105 L mol−1) and PγCD (1.49 × 105 L mol−1) ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark10)b, Table S2), showing the strongest aﬃnity

interactions of PβCD to PCS. This is consistent with the aforementioned result where PβCD exhibited larger adsorption of PCS than the other

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 7. PBUT removal of PβCD combining with hemodialysis system in a once-through mode. a) Scheme of a hemodialysis system in a once-through mode. b) PCS removal rate during hemodialysis with once-through dialysate adding with 0.5 w/w% PβCD. Removal rate of multiple uremic toxins c) PCS d) HA and e) QA co-existing in plasma during hemodialysis with once-through dialysate adding with 0.5 w/w% PβCD.

two types of PCDs. Notably, we found _K_ of PCDs binding PCS is much larger (∼ 3 orders of magnitude) than that of the corresponding monomeric CDs (Table S2), proven the outstanding binding capability of multi-pocket sites in a single PCD.

Furthermore, compared to the HSA (_K_ \= 1.0 × 105 L mol−1) ([Watanabe et al., 2012](#_bookmark51)), PβCD possesses a higher association constant and therefore is capable to compete to bind PCS over HSA. Besides, the PCS adsorption of PβCDs was an exothermic process (Figure S3), in-

dicating that the PCS binding of PCDs was temperature-dependent and low adsorption temperature is favorable to achieve a high adsorption effect.

- 1.  _PCS clearance in plasma_

To verify that PCDs improve the clearance of PCS in plasma during the dialysis, we constructed a hemodialysis system in which the dialy-sate was used in a recycled mode ([Fig. 6](#_bookmark11)a). PCS incubated with plasma was circulated in the lumen of the hollow fiber, while the dialysate with

0.5 w/w% PCD added was recycled in the opposite direction at the external of the hollow fiber ([Fig. 6](#_bookmark11)b). Blank dialysate without PCD was chosen as a negative control.

PCS removal rate quickly reached a maximum within the first 10 min for both the blank dialysate and the PCD-containing dialysate.

However, the final PCS removal rate was significantly different. While blank dialysate cleared 19.4 % of PCS, PαCD, PβCD, and PγCD-con-taining dialysates significantly enhanced the cleared portion to 41 %, 43 % and 33 %, respectively ([Fig. 6](#_bookmark11)c). PCS removal relies on the free PCS diffusion from the plasma side across the hollow fiber membrane to

the dialysate side driven by the PCS concentration difference of the two sides. PβCD possessing the best PCS adsorption capability lowers the free PCS concentration in the dialysate and subsequently increases the concentration gradient that further promotes diffusion, and therefore favorably enhances the PCS removal rate in the plasma.

To explore the optimum method for PBUT removal, we used the dialysate in a once-through mode (the dialysate passed through he-modialysis system without recirculated usage, [Fig. 7](#_bookmark12)a). PβCD was chosen as the PCS adsorbent for the further experiment, due to the highest PCS binding capability.

As shown in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark12)b, the final removal rate of PCS was about 96 %. Compared to the recycled mode, the once-through mode is a more ef-fective way that increases the removal of the PCS through lowering the PCS concentration in the dialysate and therefore produces a greater PCS concentration difference between plasma and dialysate.

To further elucidate the broad-spectrum PBUT removal properties of PβCD, PCS and other high-concentration uremic toxins in patients, hippuric acid (HA) and quinolinic acid (QA), were simultaneously

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 8. Hemocompatibility test of CDs and PCDs. a) Digital picture of hemolysis assay of CDs and PCDs. b) Hemolysis assay of CDs and PCDs.c) Plasma re-calcification time of PCDs.

added into the plasma. PCS, HA, and QA hydrophobic uremic toxins are composed of benzyl group, which allows them to bind to the hydro-phobic pocket of HSA. The removal rate of PCS, HA and QA using the blank dialysate are 66 %, 77 %, and 81 % ([Fig. 7](#_bookmark12)c-e), respectively. Compared to PCS, a higher ratio of HA and QA was removed ([Fig. 7](#_bookmark12)c-e), owing to the increasing hydrophilicity and further lower toxin-protein binding constant that allows the diffusion of more free molecules into

the dialysate, which is consistent with other reports ([Lekawanvijit,](#_bookmark31) [Kompa, Wang, Kelly, & Krum, 2012](#_bookmark31)). After adding PβCD into the dia-lysate, the removal rates of PCS (96 %), HA (98 %) and QA (97 %) were

close to 100 %, showing all the PCS, HA and QA in this system were basically removed due to host-guest interactions between the toxins and PβCD. Thus, PCD would improve the removal rate of PCS, HA and QA. Compared with the lowest removal rate of PCS obtained without adding

PβCD, the increased level of PCS removal rate obtained in present of PβCD was significantly higher than other two toxins. Compared to the single toxins present in the plasma, various additional PBUTs simulta-

neously existing in the plasma cannot affect the single toxins removal amount, showing the strong PCUT removal capability of the PCD. Taken together, PCD showed effective adsorption of various PBUTs in plasma.

So far, MOF and the activated carbon-modified membrane have been the most promising adsorbent materials to remove PCS from

plasma ([Table 1](#_bookmark8)) ([Kato et al., 2019](#_bookmark29); [Tijink et al., 2013](#_bookmark45)). PCS removal rate of activated carbon-modified membrane got to 80 % with an ad-

sorption capability of 2.68 mg g−1. In our work, the adsorption cap-ability was enhanced 3.5 fold to reach 9.24 mg g−1. PCS removal rate of MOF reached over 90 %, however, the removal was conducted at pH

6.5 ([Kato et al., 2019](#_bookmark29)), a condition not suitable for clinical application. PβCD combining with hemodialysis system in a once-through mode achieved PCS removal rate of 96 %, which is the highest removal rate so far to our best knowledge, rendering PCDs a promising PBUT adsorbent.

- 1.  _Hemocompatibility tests_

To further prove the safety of the adsorbent in case of leakage into the blood (which under normal conditions is unlikely to happen), we further evaluated the hemocompatibility of PCDs. The hemolysis rates of αCD and γCD are both below 1% ([Fig. 8](#_bookmark13)a,b), while that of βCD is about 6.4 %, in consistence with the previous report ([Xu et al., 2017](#_bookmark55)).

After polymerization, the hemolysis rates of the three PCDs were all below 1%. As the safe value of the hemolysis is 5% according to ISO10993-4 ([Li et al., 2018](#_bookmark33)), PCDs are regarded as safe and bio-compatible adsorbents ([Wei et al., 2013](#_bookmark52)).

Plasma recalcification time (PRT) was used to further identify the anticoagulant activity of PCDs. As shown in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark13)c, the PRT of PαCD, PβCD, and PγCD was 95 %, 91 %, and 98 %, respectively, suggesting

that the PCDs present in the blood would not change the coagulant activity of plasma. Combining with the hemolysis assay, even under extreme circumstances where PCDs leak into the blood, PCDs should not cause the rupture of red blood cells (Figure S4), or any additional coagulant effect of the blood.

1. Conclusion

To sum up, we fabricated PCDs via crosslinking of ECH and CDs

with similar macromolecular sizes and CD contents but different cav-ities size. We found PβCD with the appropriate cavity has the largest adsorption capability of PCS (263 mg g−1) and effectively removes not only PCS, but also other PBUTs from the blood within 2 h when com-bining with hemodialysis. Additionally, PβCD with high-eﬃcient and broad-spectrum PBUT removal properties is low-cost (less than 0.1

dollars per gram, after calculation in cost of raw materials, the ad-sorbent would spend about 7 dollars per treatment, about 15 % of local treatment cost in China.), easy to produce (one-step synthesis), highly biocompatible and applicable as a dialysate additive in existing clinical hemodialysis therapy. In summary, novel PCD adsorbent combining with hemodialysis holds promising potential for clinical PBUT removal.
